description: Combinamos perfiles complementarios en desarrollo de software full-stack, inteligencia artificial (visión por computadora, aprendizaje automático y TinyML), arquitectura cloud e infraestructura como código (AWS, Docker, Terraform) y prototipado de hardware/IoT con microcontroladores. Nos apasiona resolver problemas reales mediante soluciones tecnológicas escalables, eficientes y orientadas a la innovación espacial.
summary:
PLASPHEREx is a web tool that turns NASA's SPHEREx all-sky survey into a modern blink comparator: the same technique Clyde Tombaugh used in 1930 to find Pluto while searching for "Planet X."

SPHEREx photographs the entire sky repeatedly in infrared. PLASPHEREx lets anyone enter sky coordinates, or pick a known target, and see every SPHEREx image of that spot, streamed live from NASA/IPAC's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). The images play as an animation, so objects that move or change brightness stand out.

Beyond the animation, PLASPHEREx combines frames from each observing period into sharper epoch images. It subtracts one epoch from another to show what changed, and builds a spectrum of the target across SPHEREx's six detectors (0.75–5 µm), marking saturated measurements honestly as lower limits. Astronomer tools include blink, negative, reticle, zoom and comparison with NASA's 2010 AllWISE survey.

No installation and no coding are needed. Students, educators and amateur astronomers can repeat the method that discovered Pluto, using NASA data from this year, directly in the browser.
details:
What it does

PLASPHEREx is a public-facing web tool that turns NASA's SPHEREx all-sky survey into a modern blink comparator. It uses the same technique Clyde Tombaugh used in 1930 to discover Pluto. Users enter sky coordinates (RA/Dec, in decimal or sexagesimal), choose a field of view and one of SPHEREx's six detectors, and watch every SPHEREx image of that patch of sky play as a short video. Objects that move or change brightness stand out immediately. The five test targets from the challenge (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis) are one click away.

How it works

A Python backend queries NASA/IPAC's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) live for the SPHEREx data releases and downloads only small cutouts around the target. Each cutout is reprojected onto a common grid centered on the target, so frames align exactly. Frames are rendered with a shared contrast scale, so brightness changes are real, not artifacts. The tool offers three views:

- Frames: every observation in date order, with blink (first vs. last frame), negative, reticle, 2x zoom, full screen and PNG download.

- Epochs: frames from each six-month observing period are stacked for better signal-to-noise. Epochs are also subtracted from each other to reveal what changed.

- Spectrum: generated on the fly with aperture photometry across all six detectors (0.75–5 µm). Saturated measurements are detected from SPHEREx's quality flags and shown honestly as lower limits.

Contamination flags and saturated star cores are displayed as metadata. Each search is stored in the URL, so results can be shared or embedded. A one-click link compares the same field with NASA's 2010 AllWISE survey in CDS Aladin Lite.

Benefits and impact

No installation, accounts or coding are needed. Students, educators and amateur astronomers can repeat the method that discovered Pluto with NASA data from this year, directly in the browser. This supports the citizen-science model that has already found most known brown dwarfs, as in Backyard Worlds, and lowers the barrier for volunteers to help sift through SPHEREx's billion-object dataset.

Tools and languages

- Backend: Python, FastAPI, Astropy, Astroquery (IRSA), reproject, NumPy, with a disk cache that makes repeated searches fast. Tested with pytest and packaged with Docker.

- Frontend: JavaScript, React, Vite and Recharts.

- Exploration: Jupyter notebooks.

- Data: NASA SPHEREx via IRSA, and AllWISE via CDS Aladin.

- Cloud: Vercel for the frontend and Render for the backend.

Creativity

PLASPHEREx goes beyond showing images. It combines time (frames and epochs), change detection (blink and subtraction) and color (live spectra) in one simple interface, with the scientific care to label saturated data honestly.

Factors we considered

- Data must come live from NASA, so the tool keeps working as new SPHEREx releases arrive.

- Images must align exactly between dates and share one brightness scale, or apparent motion would be misleading.

- The interface must stay simple enough for a first-time user.

- IRSA must be respected: downloads are limited and cached.

- Larger fields of view can follow faster objects, at the cost of longer transfer times.
